newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Boutros-Ghali stepping down like deposed monarch. [CORRECTED 19:11 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Boutros-Ghali stepping down like deposed monarch. [CORRECTED 19:11 GMT]

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who will be replaced Jan. 1 by Undersecretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, steps down like a deposed monarch being sent into exile.
Proud, independent and occasionally prickly, his expected 10 year reign is being cut in half because his departure was demanded by the most powerful member of the United Nations.

The United States insists he must go because he has not done enough to reform the U.N. bureaucracy and because a tight-fisted Republican Congress will not pay more than $1 billion in back dues while he remains at the helm.
For someone born in a 100-room Cairo palace and accustomed to a starring role in the diplomatic firmament, this marks an abrupt end to an illustrious career.

When U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher proposed a face-saving one year extension earlier this year, Boutros-Ghali was reported to have rebuffed it by asking whether he was being offered "a tip."

As a Coptic Christian in Moslem Egypt, the 74-year-old Boutros-Ghali with a doctorate in international law from the Sorbonne and a string of academic distinctions had been denied the posts in his own country that his intellect, vast experience and family tradition of public service might have earned him.
His grandfather, Prime Minister Boutros Pasha Ghali, was assassinated in 1910 when Britain was Egypt's colonial ruler.

While the grandson could not aspire to head the government of an independent Egypt, he briefly held the rank of deputy prime minister for foreign affairs in 1991 after more than 13 years as minister of state for foreign affairs.

He accompanied the late President Anwar Sadat on his historic trip to Jerusalem in 1977 after Egypt's then-foreign minister resigned in protest. He then played a key role at the Camp David talks that led to the 1979 peace treaty between Egypt and Israel.

Boutros-Ghali became embroiled in a well-publicised row with the Security Council after little more than six months on the job when he said too much was being spent on U.N. peacekeeping in Bosnia and too little to assist starvation-racked Somalia.

To poverty-stricken Africans he said, Yugoslavia appeared to be "the war of the rich." On a visit to besieged Sarajevo on the last day of 1992 he was booed by demonstrators who accused him of doing too little to ease their plight.

They were even less appeased when he told a news conference that, while he accepted their frustration, "You have a situation which is better than 10 other places in the world ... Here at least you have public opinion behind you ... you have the presence of the United Nations."
Stung by criticism in the British press early on in his term, he suggested to an interviewer this was "maybe because I'm a wog" -- a pejorative term dating to colonial times.
Despite U.S. criticism for not having reined in the U.N. bureaucracy, he is widely credited with having done more to streamline the organisation than most of his predecessors.

This was as much a necessity as a virtue when the United Nations at any given time was usually owed more than $2 billion in unpaid budget dues and peacekeeping assessments -- more than half of it by the United States.

Many diplomats suggested he was jettisoned by President Bill Clinton's Democratic administration during an election year to pre-empt criticism from a Republican opposition deeply hostile to Boutros-Ghali and the United Nations.
"A useful piece of meat to throw off the sled during the election" is how the former U.N. undersecretary-General, Sir Brian Urquhart, described it.

Part of Boutros-Ghali's problem was that he was the first secretary-general appointed in the post-Cold War era. For the first time, the United Nations became involved in peacekeeping in a big way, mounting 26 often ambitious operations between 1989 and 1996, compared with 15 relatively simple monitoring missions during the previous 40 years.

Inevitably, some of the operations drew criticism, either for attempting too much or doing too little. When peacekeepers, including Americans, suffered casualties at the hands of Somali warlords and others were humiliated by Bosnian Serbs, criticism was directed at Boutros-Ghali.

"It took around 10 years to agree about the rules of the Cold War, to manage the Cold War and the institutions to apply those rules," he said in a recent interview, referring to the creation of NATO and the Warsaw Pact.
"In our case, we are still at the beginning and the member states don't know what role they want from the U.N."
